title: Parameters and return values
learningGoals: return a value from a function

youtube.title: C++ Function Parameters and Return Values | C++ Programming EP 22
youtube.description: In this episode you will pass values into a function, return a value from a function and use the returned value, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Parameters and return values · 1:19 An add function · 2:23 Values in, value out · 3:02 Second program · 4:20 Recap · 4:50 Bug of the Day · 5:44 Challenge · 6:06 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a machine with an input slot and an output tray

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today our functions take values in and send a value back. Now they can do real work.

scenes.onScreen: "Parameters and return values": numbered lines (1. Parameters are inputs; 2. Return sends one value back; 3. The caller can store the result) and an analogy card: a juice machine: you put in fruit and you get juice out
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Parameters are the inputs of a function. They sit inside the brackets, each with a type and a name. The return statement sends one value back to the caller. The type before the function name says what kind of value comes back. Think of a juice machine. You put in fruit, and you get juice out. Parameters and arguments are easy to mix up. Parameters are the names in the function line. Arguments are the real values in the call. A function can return only one value. If you need more, you will learn other tools later. A good function does one job, and its name says what the job is.
points: The caller can store the result

analogy.title: Parameters and return values
analogy.body: A juice machine: you put in fruit and you get juice out

scenes.onScreen: add.cpp: add takes two ints and returns their sum
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] The type int before the name means the function returns an int. A and b are the parameters. Each has its own type. [HL 5] Return sends the sum back to the caller. [HL 9] The call passes four and nine. Those values are called arguments. [TRACK total=13] The returned thirteen goes into total. [HL 10] Then we print it. [HL 4] The two parameters are like empty boxes. They get their values when the function is called. [HL 5] The return statement ends the function at once. Any line after it does not run. [HL 9] The order of the arguments matters. The first argument goes to the first parameter. [HL 10] The variable total holds a copy of the answer, and we print it.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: arguments go in, the result comes out
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: The call passes four and nine. The function gets them as a and b. It adds them. Then return sends thirteen back, and total stores it. Notice that the function never knows where its numbers come from. It only sees a and b. That is a big strength. You can call the same function with numbers from the keyboard, from a file or from a loop.

diagram.caption: a flow: arguments go in, the result comes out

scenes.onScreen: bigger.cpp: a function returns the bigger of two numbers
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] If a is bigger, the function returns a and ends at once. [HL 8] Otherwise it returns b. [HL 12] The first call gives twelve. [HL 13] The second call gives thirty. A function can use the same code for any two numbers. [HL 5] This is an early return. The function stops as soon as it knows the answer. [HL 8] If the first test fails, the code reaches this line. Every path through the function must end with a return. [HL 12] Now we can use the call right inside the cout line.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as bigger dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints twelve and thirty on two lines. Check the two numbers by eye. The bigger one of seven and twelve is twelve, and of thirty and five is thirty.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Parameters are the inputs of a function. Two. Return sends one value back. Three. The type before the name is the return type. Four. A return statement ends the function at once. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Parameters are the inputs of a function.
The type before the name is the return type.
A return statement ends the function at once.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: No return in a function
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The function makes a sum, but it never returns it. The compiler warns that there is no return statement in a function returning non-void. The caller gets garbage. Add return sum at the end. The compiler cannot always tell what you meant, but it can see a missing return. A function that says int must give back an int on every path. Read the warning, and look at the last line of the function.

scenes.onScreen: My function took two numbers and gave me back a headache.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: My function took two numbers and gave me back a headache.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: write a function that finds the smaller number
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function called smaller. It takes two ints and returns the smaller one. Hint: use an if inside the function, and return one of the two numbers. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: pass by value. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

add.cpp: In function 'int add(int, int)':
add.cpp:5:9: warning: unused variable 'sum' [-Wunused-variable]
    5 |     int sum = a + b;
      |         ^~~
bug.why: A function with a return type must return a value on every path. Without a return, the result is undefined.

pun: "My function took two numbers and gave me back a headache."
challenge: Write a function called smaller. It takes two ints and returns the smaller one. Hint: use an if inside the function, and return one of the two numbers.
challengeAnswer: Use an if. If a is less than b, return a. Otherwise return b. Call smaller from main and print the result.
